claims.text: Formation of a continuous, self-healing protective oxide scale is the primary factor governing oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature MPEAs.
Al and Cr are key oxide-forming elements in the proposed alloy system.
Selective segregation of Al and Cr to the alloy surface promotes formation of a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer.
A coherent, slow-growing oxide layer limits oxygen ingress.
Differences in elemental chemical potentials drive Al and Cr segregation to the surface during high-temperature exposure.
Surface enrichment in Al and Cr leads to nucleation and growth of a coherent oxide scale.
The protective oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion.
Reducing the concentration of a key oxide-forming element causes insufficient protective oxide formation.
Insufficient protective oxide formation compromises oxide-scale continuity.
A compromised oxide scale accelerates oxidation and deleterious microstructural changes.
The baseline alloy will form a more continuous and adherent oxide scale than an otherwise comparable alloy with reduced Al or Cr content.
The baseline alloy's oxide scale will grow more slowly than that of the modified alloy.
Reducing Al or Cr content will produce a more porous or discontinuous oxide scale.
Reducing Al or Cr content will increase oxidation rates and cause earlier microstructural degradation relative to the baseline.
The proposed protective-scale mechanism should govern behavior primarily from approximately 800°C to 1200°C.
At substantially lower temperatures, limited diffusion may dominate oxidation behavior.
At substantially higher temperatures, catastrophic scale spallation may dominate oxidation behavior.
Secondary phases and processing-induced defects can influence protective oxide behavior.
